payload.name: Date-specific discussion topic recovery
payload.description: When a question asks what named people discussed or the topic of a conversation on a specific date, use this to require date-aligned evidence and per-participant event searches.
content: When answering what X and Y discussed on a specific date, search each participant's individual events for that date; discussion topics are often stored as separate personal events, not as a joint 'discussion' memory.
Verify that every evidence memory's time range covers the target date; if no date-matching evidence is retrieved, run additional searches with participant names and the date before answering.
Treat 'topic' as possibly multiple topics; combine all date-matching memories rather than stopping at the first candidate.

candidates.solves: The agent failed to retrieve a participant's individual event on the target date because it searched only for a joint 'discussion' memory, then answered using a memory from a different date. The general rule is to treat date-specific discussion questions as requiring time-aligned evidence from each participant's individual events, and to never use non-date-matching evidence. This applies to any question about conversations, meetings, or shared activities on a stated date.

payload.name: Re-search post-event plans with domain terms
payload.description: When a question asks about a subject's plans after a specific event and the first search returns only the event memory, use domain/goal terms and time-bounded retrieval to locate the post-event plan memory.
content: When a question asks what plans or actions a subject has after a specific event (e.g., after advice, a meeting, a networking event), and the first search returns the event memory but no resulting plans, run an additional search using domain/goal terms inferred from the event context and the subject's goals, and restrict the time window to memories with world_start on or after the event date.
Do not answer with older, unrelated plan memories; if the re-search still yields no post-event plan memory, inspect the subject's memories dated from the event onward before finalizing an answer.

candidates.solves: Searches for post-event plans often re-use the event's keywords and miss the plan memory written in different vocabulary. When the first retrieval returns the event but no resulting plans, re-search with domain/goal terms from the event context and constrain world_start to the event date or later. Applies to any 'plans after [event]' question; not to event-description or past-state questions.

payload.name: Retrieve event date for temporal-context questions
payload.description: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with a specific event, retrieve the event and its date first, then infer the season from the date; do not stop after one search that misses the event.
content: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with an event (e.g., wedding, birthday, trip), first retrieve the event memory and its world_start date. Use event synonyms (got married/wedding, was born/birthday) and do not require the holiday or season name to appear in the query or memory text.

If the event memory provides a date but no holiday name, determine the holiday or season from the calendar date (e.g., late December → Christmas season) using general world knowledge, and answer from that date as evidence.

Do not conclude 'No information available' after a single retrieval when the question asks about an event's temporal context; run at least one additional search focused on the event and its date before answering.

candidates.solves: The runtime searched only for combined 'event + holiday' terms and stopped after one retrieval, missing the event memory whose date answers the question. The abstraction: when a question relates any dated event to a holiday or season, first retrieve the event and its date, then infer the period from the date via calendar knowledge. Applies to future questions about weddings, birthdays, trips, graduations, or similar events.

payload.name: Broaden temporal filters for time-qualified retrieval
payload.description: When a question includes a specific time or date and a point-in-time filtered search returns no direct evidence, retry with a broader time range or no time filter before concluding the information is missing.
content: When a user question contains a specific time qualifier (e.g., 'in August 2022'), do not use a point-in-time filter as a hard constraint in the initial search; use a broader time range or omit the time filter, then assess temporal relevance from memory content and timestamps.
If a point-filtered search yields no directly supporting memory, retry the same query with a wider temporal window (or no time constraint) before answering that the information is absent.

candidates.solves: The retrieval failed because a point-in-time filter set to the date in the question (August 2022) excluded a memory whose world_start was later, even though its content directly answered what was shared. This mechanism—over-trusting a question's stated time as a hard retrieval boundary—applies to any time-qualified question, especially when memory timestamps reflect update/recording time rather than event time. A general rule is to broaden or omit temporal filters before declaring an answer absent.

payload.name: Broaden kind and time filters for ongoing activity queries
payload.description: When a question asks what someone read, used, owned, or was engaged in during a time period, search across event, preference, and state memories without strict point-time filtering, because ongoing activities are often recorded as preferences or states.
content: When a query asks about an activity (reading, using, working on, owning) within a time period, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' memories that describe ongoing activities or current status.

Avoid point time_mode filters that exclude records whose world_start is near but after the target period; instead search without a strict time window first, then evaluate temporal relevance from the evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what someone read, used, owned, or was engaged in during a period, restricting retrieval to event memories with strict point-time filtering misses preference/state memories that record ongoing activities with later or loose timestamps. Use this rule for such activity-period questions, not for one-off factual queries where the target event kind and exact date are explicit.

payload.name: Temporal follow-up retrieval for sequence questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone did after, next, or following a described event, and initial results return thematically related events that may not be the actual next action.
content: When a question asks what activity followed an event (after, then, next), first locate the anchor event memory and record its timestamp and source.

Run a follow-up search for the person plus a time window starting at that timestamp, including sequence/action terms such as after, next, visited, and went; inspect memories sharing the anchor timestamp and any co-extracted events from the same source.
Before answering, verify the selected memory describes an action occurring after the anchor event and is not merely a semantically similar event from a different date; otherwise continue searching.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was answering a 'what did X do after Y' question with a thematically related but temporally unrelated memory, because retrieval ranked topic similarity over temporal adjacency. A reusable rule is to resolve sequence queries by anchoring on the prior event's timestamp and preferring memories that share or immediately follow that timestamp. This applies to any future question asking for the next action after a stated event, across all topics.

payload.name: Expand retrieval for shared personal achievements
payload.description: When a question asks what achievement or news one person shared with another, retrieve events about either person alone and use a broader time window instead of requiring both names and exact date.
content: If a query describes an item 'shared with' or 'told to' another person, search for memories whose subject is either person individually; the sharing may be implicit and the memory may mention only the achiever.
Use a broadened time window (e.g., whole stated month or relative phrases like 'last week') rather than a single point date, so recent personal milestones are not excluded.

candidates.solves: Access searches fail when a question pairs two people but the stored event records only one person's achievement or news; requiring both names and an exact point date misses memories with relative timing such as 'last week'. This rule applies to future questions about personal milestones shared between individuals, but not to questions explicitly asking for a joint or collaborative event.

payload.name: Relative-time expansion and evidence time check for temporal questions
payload.description: When a question specifies a time period and memories may store relative dates, expand searches with relative-time variants based on the session timestamp and answer only from memories whose time window overlaps asked period.
content: When a question specifies a time period (e.g., 'second week of November', 'last month'), expand search queries with the relative-time expressions equivalent to that period as measured from the session timestamp (e.g., 'last Friday', 'last week', 'this month'), because memories often store relative dates.

After retrieval, before answering a temporal question, verify each candidate memory's world_start/world_end overlaps the asked time period; discard any candidate whose time window is outside the period even if its semantic or keyword score is high, and continue searching with time-focused variants.

Do not treat memories about future interest, plans, or preferences (e.g., 'expresses interest in visiting X', 'plans to visit X') as evidence of an actual past visit; require a memory that records the event itself within the asked time window.

candidates.solves: Access failed on a temporal question because it never used relative-time variants and accepted a future-interest memory as an actual visit. The rule forces relative-time query variants from the session timestamp and requires evidence to overlap the asked period and record an actual event, not interest or plans; applies to where/when/what questions about a specified period with relative-dated memories.

payload.name: Avoid anchoring on first topic when retrieving specific events
payload.description: Use when a question about a specific past event (what someone shared/made/photographed/posted in a period) yields only partial topical matches; apply before answering to diversify queries and require direct evidence.
content: When a question asks about a specific past event (e.g., what someone shared, made, photographed, or posted in a given period) and no retrieved memory explicitly asserts the full claim (subject + object + time), do not answer from the closest topical matches.

Run at least one additional search before answering, varying the content terms: combine the subject and time window with synonyms/terms from the event's activity and likely outcome domain instead of repeating the topic that dominated the first results.
For such event questions, memories about plans, habits, preferences, or recurring topics are circumstantial; answer only when a retrieved memory directly asserts the event's object.

candidates.solves: Questions about a specific past event (what someone shared/made/photographed/posted in a period) fail when the agent anchors on a recurring topic from the first retrieval, narrows later searches to it, and answers from plan/habit memories. The rule—diversify with the event's activity/outcome terms and require direct event-specific evidence—transfers to any multi-topic subject and time-bounded event question.

payload.name: Temporal-anchor post-milestone retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did or planned after a dated milestone event (e.g., after a wedding) and the first search results appear unrelated or pre-date the event.
content: When a question asks what someone did or plans to do after a dated milestone event, use the milestone date as a temporal anchor; run searches with typical follow-up activity terms (honeymoon, celebration, get-together, trip, activity) and filter or rank memories with world_start on or after that date.
If the first retrieval returns only memories dated before the milestone, do not answer from them; re-search with additional related terms and compare time windows.
Treat pre-milestone memories as non-evidence for post-milestone questions even when they share location or activity vocabulary.

candidates.solves: Post-milestone questions fail when retrieval matches the milestone vocabulary (wedding, bride) and returns older, superficially similar memories while the true post-event activities use different terms (honeymoon, get-together) and later dates. Anchoring on the milestone date, expanding with sequel-activity vocabulary, and discarding pre-milestone memories fixes this mechanism. This applies to any 'after [event]' question about a person's activities or plans; it does not apply when the needed information predates the milestone or no milestone date is available.

payload.name: OrdinalEventDateRetrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for the date of an ordinal occurrence (e.g., third win, first visit), search broadly for base-event memories and use world_start timestamps, including relative-time references, to infer the date.
content: When a question asks when an ordinal event (second, third, nth) happened, do not search only with the ordinal and explicit date words; issue additional searches using the base event without the ordinal (e.g., 'tournament win' if asked 'third tourney win').

Treat memory world_start as date evidence even if the text expresses time relatively ('last week', 'yesterday'); use the session or message timestamp to resolve the relative reference into a concrete date before deciding.

Before answering an ordinal-date question, collect all candidate event memories from multiple searches, sort them by world_start, and identify the requested ordinal by chronological order; do not assume the only explicitly dated memory is the requested ordinal.

candidates.solves: When answering when an ordinal event (e.g., third win) occurred, retrieval often misses memories whose text uses relative time ('last week') and whose date is only in world_start; the agent then mistakes another explicitly dated event for the requested ordinal. Fix: search base event without the ordinal, treat world_start as concrete date, and order candidates chronologically to select the requested ordinal. Not applicable when a single explicit dated memory directly answers a non-ordinal question.

payload.name: Date-bounded event retrieval with count verification
payload.description: When a question asks for events within a specific date range or month, use explicit temporal filters and verify all expected events are retrieved before answering, including follow-up synonym searches when the count seems incomplete.
content: If the question specifies a date range or month, use structured or hybrid search with world_start/world_end filters covering that whole range instead of relying only on natural-language temporal phrases in the query.

Before answering a count question, verify the retrieved evidence satisfies the requested count; if not, issue additional searches using synonyms for likely milestone event types such as marriage, birth, pregnancy, move, or job change.
Do not treat a later announcement or related mention as evidence that the underlying event occurred in the target period; check the event's world_start date.

candidates.solves: Solves incomplete retrieval for questions that specify a date range or month: the system must apply explicit temporal filters and continue searching until the stated number of events is supported by evidence with world_start in the range. It does not apply to open-ended questions without temporal constraints or to construction-side memory updates.

payload.name: Time-bound retrieval for date-specific questions
payload.description: When the question contains an explicit time window (e.g., month/year), use it as a retrieval filter and only accept evidence whose recorded time falls inside that window.
content: If the question names a specific month or year, run a structured search with a temporal filter: include memories whose world_start is on or before the window end and whose world_end is null or on or after the window start.
Before using a retrieved memory as evidence, check its world_start/world_end against the question window; reject memories outside the window even if they are semantically similar.
If the first results all fall outside the window, continue searching with time-constrained queries instead of answering from the closest later memory.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about an activity, event, or state that began within a specific month or year, the agent may retrieve later semantically similar memories and answer with a different item from outside the requested timeframe. The failure mechanism is ignoring explicit temporal scope during retrieval and evidence selection. This skill applies to any time-bounded factual question over memory, not to general open-ended questions.

payload.name: Search plan memories for future attendance questions
payload.description: When a user asks when someone is attending, going to, or planning a future event, include plan memories in retrieval and expand around intention verbs.
content: When a question asks about a future or scheduled activity (e.g., 'when is X attending...', 'when will X go to...'), run retrieval with memory_kind including both 'plan' and 'event' since future intentions may be stored as plan memories with world_start dates.
If the initial results contain no direct date, re-query with expansions such as 'plans to attend', 'will attend', 'scheduled to attend', 'next month/week' and do not restrict to event kind.
Use the world_start of a retrieved plan memory as the temporal anchor for answering 'when' questions.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because retrieval filtered to event memories only, missing a plan memory that recorded a future conference date. Temporal 'when' questions about upcoming activities require searching plan memories alongside events, since plan memories carry world_start dates. This applies to any future question asking when an entity will attend, visit, or participate in something.

payload.name: Time-bounded plural recall search
payload.description: When a question asks for all items within a specific time period, use a time-filtered structured search and verify completeness before answering.
content: If the question contains a time constraint (e.g., a month/year or date range), issue a structured search that filters memories by world_start/world_end falling within that period; relevant memories may use relative time and lack literal date words.

When the question uses a plural target noun (e.g., places, events, people), treat the answer as potentially multi-valued; after the first search, judge whether the evidence set is complete and run additional searches (e.g., broader keywords or time-range filter) before answering.
Resolve relative time expressions in memories (e.g., 'last month', 'last week') against the message/session timestamp to decide if they fall inside the requested period.

candidates.solves: This addresses incomplete retrieval when answering time-bounded recall questions that expect multiple items. The diagnosed cause was that a memory mentioning a target location was missed because it used a relative time expression and lacked literal date keywords, while the search relied only on keyword/semantic expansion. The abstraction is a decision rule to use structured time-range filters and completeness checks, applicable to any future question with an explicit time window and a plural recall target.

payload.name: Date-specific retrieval follow-up
payload.description: When a query asks about an event on a specific date and the first memory search returns no event on that date, run an additional search using the date and subject before answering no information.
content: If a user question contains a concrete date and a subject (person/entity), and your initial retrieval returned no memory whose world_start matches that date, perform at least one additional search that combines the subject with the date as a keyword or structured filter before answering 'no information'.
Do not rely only on semantic similarity for date-specific questions; use date-filtered or keyword retrieval to catch events whose phrasing differs from the query.

candidates.solves: When a date-specific question retrieves no memory for that date, the agent often gives up after one hybrid search, even though an event memory with the exact date exists but ranked below the cutoff. Perform at least one additional date-and-subject filtered or keyword search before concluding no information; this applies to any future 'what happened on [date] for [person/entity]' query.

payload.name: Time-range search for period questions
payload.description: When a user asks about activities/classes/events that happened or started in a period (e.g., mid-August, during June), search with a time_range covering the full period and query expansions for started/enrolled/joined.
content: For questions that name a time period (e.g., mid-August 2023, early June, during 2023), use a time_range spanning the full period instead of a single point-in-time target, so events whose start date falls later in the period are still retrieved.
Expand searches for enrollment/activity questions with verbs like started, began, joined, enrolled, took, and include event/state memory kinds to match memories phrased as 'started taking X classes'.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what events, classes, or activities occurred or started within a named period (e.g., 'mid-August', 'last week'), a point-in-time search at the period's midpoint can exclude later-starting events, causing missed answers. Use a full-period time_range and expand verbs like started/enrolled/joined; do not apply this when the question specifies an exact calendar date/time point.

payload.name: Temporal consistency check before answering
payload.description: When a question specifies a time period for an event, verify each retrieved memory's world_start/world_end overlaps the period before using it as evidence; re-search with time filters if top candidates are temporally inconsistent.
content: When the question specifies a time window, before answering check every candidate memory's world_start/world_end and discard any whose range does not overlap the window, even if the text seems semantically relevant.

If no valid evidence remains, re-search with a structured time filter (e.g., world_start within the window) and broaden activity verbs (trip, visit, retreat, vacation) instead of repeating only the exact wording from the question.
Never answer using a memory whose date contradicts the question's timeframe unless another retrieved memory explicitly places the event inside the window.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was answering a time-bounded question with a semantically similar memory whose date was outside the window. The reusable fix is to check each candidate's world_start/world_end against the question's period before answering, and re-search with time-filtered queries plus broader activity terms when candidates are temporally invalid. Applies to any future question that anchors an event to a date range.

payload.name: Verify explicit event timing evidence
payload.description: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started), require evidence that explicitly states that event's timing; do not substitute a related event's date (publication, exhibit, announcement).
content: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started, created), verify the cited memory explicitly describes that event and its timing. Do not answer with the date of a related event (publication, exhibition, announcement) unless a memory explicitly equates that date with the requested event's time.

If retrieved memories only concern related events or lack explicit timing for the requested event, judge the evidence insufficient and run additional searches using temporal/completion phrases (e.g., 'completed', 'finished', 'a few days ago', 'recently') and structured filters on the relevant subject/predicate (e.g., artwork/created/completed).

When a search returns a memory with explicit relative timing (e.g., 'a few days ago'), resolve the date from the memory/session timestamp and cite that memory as evidence rather than the related-event memory.

candidates.solves: Questions asking when a specific event happened (completion, finish, start) fail when the agent uses a related event's date (publication, exhibition, announcement) or answers without explicit timing evidence. The rule requires explicit temporal evidence for the requested event and adds completion-focused supplementary searches, applying to any 'when did X finish/complete Y' question across topics.

payload.name: Attribute-synonym search expansion
payload.description: When a question asks for a specific attribute value (breed, type, color, age) of an entity and initial searches return only generic mentions, re-search with synonym families of the attribute and likely value descriptors before answering.
content: When a user asks for a specific attribute (breed, type, color, age, etc.) of an entity and retrieved memories mention the entity but none explicitly state the attribute, run additional searches using synonym families of the attribute and common value descriptors (e.g., mix, mutt, cross for breed; approximate age phrases for age) instead of repeating the question's exact wording.

After each expanded search, inspect the full text of candidate memories, including their subject and object fields, for any explicit attribute statement; use only evidence from retrieved/current versions when answering, and if the value is still absent, say it is not found rather than guessing.

candidates.solves: Questions asking for a concrete attribute (breed, type, color, age) of an entity can miss memories that phrase the value differently (e.g., 'mutt/mix' vs 'breeds'), so generic searches return only entity-level mentions. This rule requires synonym-family expansion of the attribute and likely value descriptors before answering, surfacing such memories without knowing the answer. Applies to any entity-attribute query; not needed when explicit values are already retrieved.

payload.name: SearchShortPhrasesWithBaseNoun
payload.description: When a question asks for a short attribute like a motto, slogan, nickname, or title, include the standalone base noun in keyword searches and try a semantic/hybrid search if the exact phrase misses.
content: If the query asks about a short named attribute (motto, slogan, nickname, title), add the bare noun (e.g., 'motto') as a keyword in addition to any full phrase like 'family motto'.

When the first keyword search does not return a memory containing that attribute word, re-run with the base word alone and also perform a semantic or hybrid search before concluding no information is available.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because a keyword search for 'family motto' missed an existing memory containing 'family's motto' — the possessive form blocked exact phrase matching. Future questions about short attributes such as a motto, slogan, nickname, or title face the same risk when the stored text uses a possessive or inflected variant. This rule applies when the target is a retrievable short phrase; it does not apply when the answer must be synthesized from multiple facts.

payload.name: Category-instance search diversification
payload.description: When a question asks for instances of a category (e.g., activities, hobbies, interests, foods) and initial retrieval yields no clear instance, run additional searches with concrete candidate terms and synonyms, not repeated identical queries.
content: When a question asks to enumerate instances of a category (activities, hobbies, interests, foods, etc.), derive candidate instance terms from the question, from any retrieved memories, and from common subcategories; run separate searches for each candidate term combined with the subject.

If a search for category instances returns only peripherally related memories (e.g., a company, a place) and no concrete instance, reformulate the query with synonyms and specific examples of the category before concluding; do not rerun the same query with only depth or top_k changed.

candidates.solves: The agent failed to retrieve a memory naming a concrete outdoor activity because it repeated the same category-label query with only depth changed. Category-enumeration questions (activities, hobbies, interests, features, items) often have evidence stored under specific instance terms rather than the category label, so retrieval must diversify into candidate instance terms. This applies to any future question asking for examples of a category; it does not apply to single-entity lookups or when evidence is explicitly labeled.

payload.name: Value-based retrieval for post-career role questions
payload.description: When a question asks what a person could do after a current career and no explicit plan is found, also search for values, interests, and teaching/helping/leadership activities.
content: If the question asks about a person's possible future role after a known career and the initial search returns no explicit plan, run extra searches for the person's values, interests, and past activities involving leadership, teaching, giving back, or helping others.
Use only retrieved evidence for such values and activities when proposing plausible future roles; do not invent unsupported facts.

candidates.solves: For open-ended questions asking what a person could do after a known career, a single career-focused search can miss memories about the person's values, interests, and helping/teaching/leadership activities that support an inferred answer. The fix is to require additional value/activity searches before answering. This applies to any person/career subject, but not to questions asking for explicit factual career paths already stated in memory.

payload.name: Retrieve Generic Creative Work Descriptions
payload.description: When a question asks what a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project) is about, use before hybrid search to also query generic descriptors like 'creative project' and 'completed project' and inspect event/achievement memories.
content: When the user asks about the subject of a specific creative work, do not restrict search to the exact artifact term and ordinal; include query expansions and keywords using generic descriptors such as 'creative project', 'completed project', 'recent work', plus thematic/content words from the question.

If initial results contain no memory stating the completed work's subject, search or inspect event memories with predicates like achievement or completion rather than only in-progress plans or titles, since completed works may be stored generically.

Judge evidence sufficiency against all retrieved current related memories, not only those mentioning the exact artifact type; a memory describing a completed creative project with matching themes can satisfy the question.

candidates.solves: Retrieval misses the answer when a memory encodes a completed creative work in generic terms ('creative project') rather than by its specific type ('screenplay'), so a query anchored on 'third screenplay' fails to surface it. Future questions about the subject of any specific creative work should broaden retrieval to generic project/completion descriptors and thematic keywords before concluding evidence is missing.

payload.name: ComplementQueryForBesidesQuestions
payload.description: When the user asks for activities, hobbies, or interests besides/apart from an explicitly named topic, use structured and expanded searches that do not let that topic dominate.
content: When the question asks for activities, hobbies, or interests 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' an explicitly named topic (e.g., yoga), do not build the main query around that topic, or results will be dominated by memories about it.

Construct the query around the general category (e.g., 'activities', 'hobbies', 'interests', 'pursuits') while omitting the excluded topic, and include concrete alternative terms from the person's known context.

Use structured search with relevant predicates (e.g., predicate='activity') to retrieve diverse activity memories, and increase top_k or issue multiple searches with varied expansions so less central activities are not crowded out.

After retrieval, discard memories whose content is primarily about the excluded topic, check whether the retrieved set covers distinct concrete activities, and if not, search again with additional expansions.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for activities or interests besides an explicitly named dominant topic, retrieval tends to return memories centered on that topic and misses quieter alternative activities. This rule forces the search to drop the excluded term, use structured predicate filters, and broaden top-k/expansions so diverse activities are retrieved. Applies to any entity/topic in future questions phrased with 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than'.

payload.name: DualSearchForRecommendations
payload.description: When a question asks for a hobby, activity, or recommendation related to a person's stated interest, use this Skill to search for existing hobbies/skills in addition to the interest and consider combinations.
content: When a question asks for a recommendation related to a stated interest, run at least two semantic searches: one for the stated interest with recommendation keywords, and one for the person's existing skills, activities, and hobbies without referencing the interest.

If the first search returns only surface matches (e.g., travel clubs) and no clear integrated candidate, expand queries to combine the found skills with the interest (e.g., 'writing about travel', 'travel blogging') before answering.
Before answering, verify that retrieved evidence contains both the stated interest and a relevant existing activity; if not, issue additional searches rather than answering from partial evidence.

candidates.solves: When a user asks for a recommendation (hobby, activity, gift) related to a stated interest, the agent tends to search only for that interest and retrieves surface matches, missing the person's existing complementary skills that would form the best recommendation. This rule forces dual retrieval (interest + existing hobbies/skills) and combination queries, which applies to any such recommendation question across topics.

payload.name: activity-participation_search_for_hobbies
payload.description: Use when answering questions about what hobbies, interests, or new activities a person considered, tried, or enjoys; run complementary searches with participation phrasing (e.g., 'attends a class', 'enjoys [activity]') and concrete activity terms before answering.
content: When the question asks about hobbies, interests, or activities a person considered/tried/enjoys, do not answer after a single search phrased with meta-labels like 'considered trying'. Run at least one additional search using participation frames: '[subject] attends/is taking/learns [activity]', '[subject] enjoys [activity]', '[subject] is practicing [activity]'.

For each candidate activity surfaced in any retrieved memory (including classes, sports, or pastimes), search for that concrete activity name, and include preference/event/plan memory kinds covering interests, recreation, and intents.

Before finalizing the answer, verify that the evidence covers all activities the user asks about; if retrieved results contain only general descriptions without concrete activity names, issue broader complementary searches rather than answering from partial evidence.

candidates.solves: When a user asks which hobbies or activities a person considered or tried, memories often encode the activity as participation ('attending a class', 'enjoys running') rather than with words like 'hobby' or 'consider'. A single meta-language hybrid search can miss these memories. Future equivalent questions require complementary searches using activity-participation phrasing and concrete activity terms before answering.

payload.name: Search broader interests when asking for alternatives after a domain
payload.description: When a question asks what alternative career/path someone might consider after a stated activity/domain, also retrieve that person's other interests, hobbies, knowledge, and activities outside that domain before answering.
content: If the question asks what alternative career or path someone might consider after a named activity/domain, do not limit retrieval to that domain. Run at least one additional search using the person's other hobbies, interests, knowledge, routines, and activities (e.g., pet care, volunteering, creative work) as query terms.

Before answering, check whether any retrieved evidence outside the named domain shows relevant skill or enjoyment; if present, ground the answer in that evidence rather than only in memories from the named domain.

candidates.solves: An access run failed because the query for an alternative career after a named activity was expanded only within that activity's domain, so memories about the person's other knowledge and enjoyment were never retrieved. The same overly narrow query formulation recurs whenever a user asks what else a person might do after a current role or interest. Searching the subject's broader hobbies, skills, and activities before answering is a transferable retrieval rule for such alternative-option questions.

payload.name: Retrieve activities for experience-based advice
payload.description: When a question asks what advice or lessons a person would give based on their experiences or personal growth, also search for their hobbies, interests, and stress-relieving activities, not only explicit advice memories.
content: When the question asks what advice, lessons, or recommendations someone would give based on their experiences or personal growth, do not rely only on explicit advice/support memories. Run additional searches for the person's hobbies, interests, and stress-relieving activities, prioritizing 'preference' and 'event' memories about pastimes such as outdoor, creative, or travel activities.

Before answering, verify whether the retrieved evidence includes such activity memories; if not, issue a new varied search with activity-oriented keywords and treat the found activities as evidence for the advice.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what advice a person would give based on their experiences or growth, retrieval often targets explicit advice/support statements and misses the person's hobbies and stress-relieving activities that ground the advice. This rule adds activity/preference searches so the answer reflects what actually helps the person. Applies to any advice-from-experience question; not applicable when the question asks only for explicitly stated facts or opinions.

payload.name: Include preference memories for hobby questions
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's hobby, interest, or long-term activity (e.g., 'started practicing a few years ago', 'enjoys doing'), apply this before searching memory.
content: When the question targets a hobby, interest, or long-term activity, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' (and other relevant kinds) because such facts are often stored as preference records.

If the first event-only search does not surface a memory that explicitly names the hobby and its duration, retry with memory_kinds including 'preference' (and 'profile'/'state' as appropriate), and avoid a time range that excludes older preference records.
Treat a preference memory that states the hobby and how long the person has enjoyed it as sufficient evidence; do not require a matching event entry.

candidates.solves: A hobby question failed because search was restricted to event memory kinds, missing the relevant preference memory. Fix: for questions about enduring hobbies/interests and their duration, include preference-kind memories, not only events. Applies to future questions about long-standing interests/hobbies; does not apply to questions about a specific dated one-time event.

payload.name: Retrieve interests for which-activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks which activity or hobby gives a person a benefit (e.g., escape, relaxation, imagination), retrieve the person's known interests from profile or preference memories and use them as candidate search terms.
content: When a question asks which activity or hobby gives a person a benefit, do not limit retrieval to memories that explicitly contain the benefit words. Retrieve the person's known hobbies/interests from profile or preference memories and treat them as candidate activities.
Before answering, run an additional memory search for each known interest/hobby term, and consider those results even if the benefit words are absent from the returned memory text.
If several interest memories compete, compare them using direct preference statements, frequency, and recency before selecting the answer.

candidates.solves: The answer was in a profile memory listing interests, but retrieval only matched memories explicitly containing the benefit words, producing a wrong activity. This rule generalizes to 'which activity' questions where the benefit is described in words not present in the correct memory; it applies by adding known interests as candidate searches. It does not apply to specific dated events or when the correct memory already contains the benefit wording.

payload.name: Instance-list retrieval for category questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for specific examples/instances of a category (games, movies, books, foods, hobbies) for a subject, and the first generic search returns only broad statements without named items.
content: If a question asks for a list of specific items of a category (e.g., games, movies, books, hobbies) associated with a subject, and an initial generic-category search returns only broad descriptions without naming any items, do not end the search yet.

Run additional targeted searches combining the subject's name with category-related activity terms (e.g., 'plays', 'watched', 'recommends', 'enjoys', 'won'), and also search for the category itself in conjunction with related contexts (e.g., 'tournament', 'recommendation'). Inspect event, achievement, and preference memories because they often contain the specific named items.
Only produce 'No information available' after multiple varied searches fail to surface any specific named instances.

candidates.solves: The agent answered 'no information' after a single generic category search missed memories that name specific games in event and activity entries. The mechanism is that category-instance questions require iterative, instance-oriented searching because supporting memories often mention concrete names without repeating the category word. This applies to any future question asking for a list of concrete items associated with a subject, across topics like games, movies, books, and hobbies.

payload.name: Search beyond excluded activity for alternatives
payload.description: When a question asks what activity a person or group planned/did instead of a known activity, use this to avoid over-anchoring retrieval on the excluded activity.
content: If the user asks for an alternative, replacement, or activity done instead of a previously mentioned activity, do not build all searches and keywords around the excluded activity; the supporting memory may omit that activity entirely.

Run additional searches using the subject person/group plus substitution intent terms such as 'instead', 'alternative', 'planned to', and 'decided to', and search broadly for shared plans, preferences, or recent events involving the same people.

Before answering, inspect retrieved memories that mention plans or shared activities for those people even if they do not mention the excluded activity; select the memory that explicitly states the alternative plan rather than the first semantically similar result.

candidates.solves: Retrieval fails when a question asks what someone did or planned instead of a known activity, because search is over-anchored on the excluded activity and the supporting memory only describes the replacement activity without mentioning the excluded one. This skill applies to any future 'instead / alternative / replacement / rather than' retrieval task; it does not apply to straightforward factual questions that do not involve an explicit contrast.

payload.name: Non-primary goal search across memory kinds
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's goals, plans, or aspirations that are distinct from their primary skill/domain, include preference, event, and plan memory kinds and search concrete non-primary activity terms before answering.
content: When answering questions about a person's goals, aspirations, career plans, or intentions (especially goals distinct from their primary skill), do not restrict retrieval to only 'profile' and 'state' memory kinds. Include 'preference', 'event', and 'plan' kinds, because goals and off-the-field ambitions are commonly stored there.

When the question contrasts goals with the person's main domain, search with concrete terms for that person's non-primary activities (e.g., endorsements, charity, brand, business, community) in addition to negated goal phrases, and inspect memories that mention these activities even if initial scores are low.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that repeated hybrid searches restricted memory_kinds to 'profile' and 'state' and used only negated goal phrases, so the answer-holding 'preference' and 'event' memories were never retrieved. This skill abstracts a reusable retrieval rule: when a question asks about a person's goals or aspirations distinct from their primary skill/domain, broaden memory-kind coverage and search concrete non-primary activity terms before concluding. Applies to any future non-primary goal or ambition question.

payload.name: Exhaustive retrieval for category enumeration questions
payload.description: When a user asks for a list of items in a category (hobbies, interests, activities, possessions, preferences, etc.), use this skill before answering.
content: Before answering an enumeration-of-category question, run multiple searches with distinct query formulations and keywords targeting the category and its possible sub-items; do not stop after the first hybrid search.

Inspect results from all memory kinds (preference, event, plan, profile) and include any memory that mentions the subject's engagement, interest, or intention regarding the category, even if the memory's main topic is different.
Continue searching until an additional search returns no new distinct candidate members, then aggregate the full set into the answer and cite all supporting evidence.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask to enumerate the members of a category (hobbies, interests, activities, possessions, preferences) are often answered from the first retrieval batch, which misses items stored in plans, events, and preferences using different vocabulary. This skill supplies a decision rule: exhaustively search multiple query angles and all memory kinds before answering, so the final answer aggregates every relevant candidate.

payload.name: Origin-focused retrieval for introduction questions
payload.description: When a question asks how someone was introduced to, started, or first became involved in an activity, run an origin-focused search before answering.
content: If the user asks how a person was introduced to or started an activity/interest, do not answer from current-state memories about that activity alone.

Run an additional search with origin-oriented expansions (e.g., 'since childhood', 'first started', 'introduced by', 'early years') and inspect composite memories that mention family or early context even if their main topic is unrelated.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: origin/introduction questions return only current-state memories about the activity, missing composite memories with early-life context (e.g., 'since childhood, starting with father...'). The rule adds a second retrieval pass using origin cues (started, introduced by, since childhood, first) and requires inspecting composite memories before answering. This generalizes to any 'how did X start/get introduced to Y' question and does not apply to questions about current engagement.

payload.name: Per-person profile search for shared-interest questions
payload.description: When a question asks what interests, hobbies, or preferences two or more people share, search each person's profile/hobby memories separately before answering.
content: When the question asks what two or more named people share (interests, hobbies, preferences, or similar traits), run a separate profile/hobby search for each person (e.g., query with the person's name and 'hobbies' or 'interests') in addition to a joint-activity search.

Do not treat plans to do something together, one-time joint events, or supportive gestures as evidence of a shared interest; require either an explicit shared-interest memory or overlapping individual profile/preference memories.
After initial retrieval, judge evidence sufficiency for the comparison: if the evidence only describes activities done or planned together, run the per-person profile searches again before answering.

candidates.solves: A single joint-activity query for shared interests can miss each person's profile hobby memories, yielding answers based on plans or events. Fix: for common-attribute questions across named people, run per-person profile/hobby searches and intersect. Not for single-person questions or when an explicit shared-interest memory exists.

payload.name: Search general hobbies for activity-during-period questions
payload.description: When a question asks what activity a person does during a specific time or condition (e.g., while healing, during recovery, in their free time), before answering, also search for that person's general hobbies, interests, or pastimes without repeating the time/condition qualifier.
content: If a user asks what activity someone does during a stated period or condition (e.g., while healing, during vacation, on weekends), run a supplementary memory search with queries like '<person> hobbies', '<person> interests', and '<person> activities' without the period qualifier. Such preferences are often stored independently of the period.
When judging evidence sufficiency for these questions, do not require memories to mention the period; a hobby or pastime stated generally can be the correct activity during that period.

candidates.solves: Retrieval over-anchors on a temporal or situational qualifier (e.g., 'while healing his knee'), ranking event memories about the condition and missing a general hobby memory that holds the answer. Future questions that ask what activity a person does during a stated period should trigger an additional qualifier-free search for the person's general hobbies, interests, or pastimes, because the relevant memory may be stored without reference to the period.

payload.name: ExpandSearchForOngoingCreativeWork
payload.description: When a question asks what kind of fiction, stories, or creative work someone writes or creates, and the first search returns only interests, preferences, or older writings, run additional event-focused searches before answering.
content: Before answering what kind of stories or creative work someone produces, treat a single literal-query search as insufficient if it returns only preferences, interests, or older articles.
Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search for recent event memories using phrases such as 'currently working on', 'writing', 'struggling with', or 'challenge'.
If a recovered event memory explicitly describes the current work and a notable feature that directly answers the question, include that feature in the answer.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what kind of fiction or creative work someone writes, a single literal-query search often misses recent event memories describing current work and distinctive features, returning only preferences or older writings. The rule adds an event-focused search before answering, applying to future questions about ongoing creative output, not to stated preferences or historical reading habits.

payload.name: Count_questions_search_ownership_verbs
payload.description: When a question asks how many of a category a person has or owns as of a time, and generic category+'count' searches miss ownership records, also search with acquisition/possession verbs and discovered instance names.
content: When answering 'how many X does Y have as of [time]', do not stop after searches combining X and 'count'/'number'; ownership evidence often appears in event memories as verbs (adopted, bought, got, received, owns, has).
If initial retrievals lack ownership records, run additional keyword/BM25 searches joining Y with each acquisition/possession verb and the category X (e.g., '[Y] adopted X', '[Y] owns X').
When any retrieved memory names an instance (e.g., a pet name), also search for that instance alongside Y and X to discover co-occurring other instances before finalizing the count.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that count-of-possessions questions under-recall because memory events use acquisition verbs (adopted, bought) and instance names rather than the category noun plus 'count'. This rule requires verb-based and instance-based supplementary searches when generic category+count searches miss. It applies to any future question enumerating concrete owned or acquired entities (pets, vehicles, children) by a specified person as of a date, not to preference or plan questions.

payload.name: Enumerate purchases with category vocabulary search
payload.description: When a question asks what items someone bought or made for a beneficiary class (pets, children, home, etc.), search using the full set of typical item terms for that class, not just already-retrieved items.
content: Before answering an enumeration question about items bought/created for a beneficiary class (e.g., pets, children, household), identify the class and generate a broad list of concrete category items (for pets: beds, collars, tags, toys, leashes, food, grooming supplies; for children: clothes, toys, books, furniture).
Run at least one additional keyword or hybrid search using these category terms even if prior searches returned memories, and inspect any newly retrieved candidates before finalizing the answer.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate items a person bought or made for a beneficiary class (e.g., their pets, children, home), retrieval can miss common items because queries are seeded only with items already found. This causes incomplete answers like missing 'dog beds' when searches used 'toys, goodies, jewelry'. The rule is to generate and search the typical category vocabulary of that beneficiary class (e.g., for pets: beds, collars, tags, toys, leashes, food) before concluding, which applies to any future enumeration question about purchases or creations for a group.

payload.name: Expand list answers from implied work mentions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a list/set of entities (authors, books, people, places) and retrieved memories mention specific works or items that could imply additional list members. Apply before finalizing an answer, after initial retrieval, to expand queries and infer implied entities.
content: When the question asks for a list or set of entities (e.g., authors, books, participants) and initial retrieval returns only one explicit match, do not finalize. Search again using terms derived from the returned memories (titles, names, series) and the target relationship (e.g., author of <title>).

If a memory mentions a well-known work or item (book, movie, product), treat its creator/author/owner as a candidate list member only if other retrieved evidence supports the connection; otherwise keep it as a query expansion.
Repeat search/inspection until additional query variations yield no new supported candidates, then answer with the full set of distinct members supported by visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for all members of a set and the first search finds only one explicit match, the agent answers too early. The cause is that memories referencing well-known works (e.g., a book title) imply additional set members (their authors) without containing the query words. The rule uses such mentions as query expansions, infers the implied entity, and continues searching until no new supported candidate appears. This applies to plural list questions, not single-fact questions or entities unsupported by memory.

payload.name: Expand_event_synonyms_before_no_information
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many times an event happened and the first search returns no explicit matches; expand synonym-phrased searches before concluding no information.
content: Before answering 'no information' for an event-count question, run additional keyword or hybrid searches with morphological variants and synonyms of the event term (e.g., rejected → rejection, declined, setback) and related object terms.

Do not treat a single failed keyword search as proof that an event never occurred; expand the query to the subject's associated activities and roles, then re-judge evidence sufficiency before concluding absence.

candidates.solves: Stored events used different wording ('rejection letter', 'setback') than the searched keyword ('rejected'), and the agent stopped after one search. The reusable failure is giving up too early on event-count questions when surface forms differ. Expanding synonyms and related object terms before declaring absence applies to any future count/enumeration question (how many times X happened), not when explicit evidence is already retrieved.

payload.name: Compare entities via per-entity factual searches
payload.description: When a question asks what two or more named entities have in common or what they both share, retrieve factual state/event memories for each entity individually and compare, instead of relying on one abstract similarity query.
content: If the question asks what two or more named entities have in common (e.g., 'what do X and Y both...'), do not rely on a single abstract similarity search. Issue separate searches for each named entity targeting their factual state/event memories (job, career, business, education, residence, major life changes).

After per-entity searches, identify overlapping facts across the entities and answer only from those retrieved memories. If the initial results contain only relationship/support memories without factual states, treat evidence as insufficient and search again for each entity's life-event and state memories.

When a generic semantic query fails to surface factual commonalities, use structured or keyword strategies with each entity's name plus domain predicates (e.g., 'lost job', 'started business', 'owns') to find comparable factual memories.

candidates.solves: Comparative questions such as 'what do X and Y have in common' fail when the agent runs only one abstract similarity query, which surfaces relational/support memories but not each person's factual life events. Diagnosed cause: the query 'common characteristics' missed memories about job loss and starting businesses. Abstract mechanism: generic comparative queries under-retrieve per-entity facts. This rule applies to any future comparison, overlap, or shared-attribute question about named entities, requiring per-entity factual retrieval before answering.

payload.name: List-made-items-retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks to list items a person has made, cooked, or created (e.g., recipes, dishes), apply before answering to run multiple targeted searches that surface specific named items.
content: When the user asks what items a person has made or created, treat it as an enumeration query; do not answer after one generic search.

Run multiple searches: one with the person's name plus action verbs (made, baked, cooked, prepared, created), one with the item category and the person's name, and one for the person's preferences or favorites that may name specific items.

Before answering, verify the retrieved evidence contains specific named items; if not, continue with additional keyword or structured searches using known details (e.g., ingredients, flavors) rather than stopping with generic descriptions.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate what a person has made or created (e.g., recipes, dishes, projects), a single generic query often misses specific named items stored in event or preference memories. This skill addresses the general failure of retrieval completeness for enumeration questions by requiring multiple targeted searches with action verbs and preference memories, applicable to any future 'what has X made' request.

payload.name: Per-entity expansion for intersection queries
payload.description: Use when a question asks what two or more entities share (e.g., both visited, both like, common plan) and initial retrieval misses evidence or returns only generic memories.
content: If the initial search for a multi-entity intersection query returns no overlap, do not repeat the identical query; issue separate searches for each entity using its name and known aliases.

After each per-entity search, collect concrete attribute values (cities, activities, preferences) from retrieved memories and issue follow-up searches combining each entity with those candidate values.
Conclude 'no information' only after per-entity searches for all entities and candidate-value expansions have been attempted and still yield no supporting memory.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an intersection or common attribute (e.g., a city both people visited) and the initial hybrid search returns only generic memories for one entity or no overlap, the failure mechanism is searching only the combined query and never issuing per-entity searches with name variants and candidate attribute values. Future equivalent questions benefit by decomposing the query per entity and expanding with concrete values found in retrieved memories before concluding no evidence.

payload.name: Enumerative attribute retrieval with per-category searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks what kinds/types/forms of a thing a person produces, creates, or engages in, and the first search returns generic results.
content: Before answering enumeration questions, split the requested attribute into likely concrete categories (e.g., screenplay/script, book, blog/post, journal, article, poem) and run a separate search for each category, not only the general phrase.
When a memory mentions a specific completed or ongoing artifact of a category, treat it as evidence for that category even if the memory's main topic is another event or experience.
Do not answer an enumeration question after only one top-k search; if additional category searches return no supporting memory, state only the categories with visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for all kinds/types of a person's outputs or activities (e.g., writings, creative works, projects), a single top-k hybrid search usually returns only generic or partially matching memories and misses concrete event instances such as completed works, posts, or journals. This skill instructs the agent to enumerate likely categories and run additional targeted searches for each, and to treat concrete event/plan memories mentioning specific formats as evidence, avoiding incomplete answers.

payload.name: Decompose multi-condition retrieval queries
payload.description: When a question asks for an activity or item satisfying two independent conditions (e.g., a person's enjoyment AND benefit to their pet), run separate targeted searches for each condition before combining.
content: When a question requires intersecting two independent facts about a subject (e.g., an activity they enjoy AND a pet they own), run separate retrieval passes: one per condition. Do not rely on a single combined query.
Vary query terms per pass: for enjoyment/hobbies use terms like enjoys, getting into, trying, hobby, activity; for possession/relationship use terms like adopted, has, owns, pet, dog.
Answer only when evidence covers both conditions. If one side is missing, issue additional targeted searches for that condition before finalizing.

candidates.solves: Access failures occur when compound questions require evidence from two independent memory dimensions (e.g., a person's current hobby and their pet ownership) but the agent runs only one combined query that misses one dimension. This skill instructs decomposing such questions into separate sub-queries and verifying evidence for each condition before answering. It applies to any future question asking for an activity or item that must satisfy both a subject preference and a relationship/possession fact, so long as a single memory does not already record the combined activity.

payload.name: Count owned items via acquisition events
payload.description: When asked how many of an item a person has/owns, search for individual acquisition/ownership events before concluding missing information; do not rely on number/count phrasing.
content: If a question asks for a count of items a person owns/has, search for concrete acquisition or ownership events: adopted, bought, received, owns, has a [item], or named instances of the item.
Do not make 'number', 'count', or 'how many' the primary query terms; these often miss individual event memories.
Enumerate distinct named entities/instances from retrieved memories and sum them only when each event clearly indicates a separate item owned by the person.
If retrieval returns only plans, considerations, or other people's items, continue searching with alternative terms before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: counting questions fail when retrieval targets the numeric phrasing (e.g., 'how many dogs does X have') and misses individual acquisition/ownership events that establish each owned item. The reusable mechanism applies to any future question asking how many of an item a person has, owns, or has adopted; the count must be assembled from separate event memories, not from a single explicit total. Boundary: not needed when the answer is already stored as an explicit count in one memory.

payload.name: Exhaustive retrieval for counting questions
payload.description: When a question asks how many times or the total number of events a person participated in (e.g., tournaments, competitions), keep searching with varied queries until no new relevant memories are found, then aggregate all distinct events before answering.
content: When the question asks for a count or number of an entity's activities, treat it as an exhaustive count: do not stop after the first top-k search.
Issue additional searches using synonyms and related terms (e.g., 'won', 'participated', 'tournament', 'competition') and increase top-k/depth until the last search returns no new relevant memories.

Before answering, aggregate every distinct event memory that matches the counted activity; verify that the answer equals the total number of distinct events found, not just the first retrieved subset.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a count question was answered from a single top-k search, missing several relevant event memories. The reusable mechanism is that numeric questions about an entity's activities require exhaustive retrieval and aggregation, not a first-pass subset. This applies whenever a future question asks for a count or total of an entity's events, across any topic.

payload.name: Expand frustration queries to unmet-need evidence
payload.description: When a question asks about a frustration, problem, or difficulty, expand retrieval to memories of unmet needs or ongoing searches (e.g., 'searching for X but has not found one') rather than only literal emotion words.
content: When the question uses an emotional label such as 'frustration', 'problem', or 'difficulty', do not search only those literal words; add expansions that capture the underlying situation: 'searching for', 'looking for', 'has not found', 'unable to find', 'struggling with', 'wants to find'.

For a stated 'shared' or common experience, include targeted searches on the relationship between the named people and on each person's events about the same topic; the memory may describe only one person's unmet need that the other supports.

If the first search returns no direct match, issue at least one alternate retrieval (keyword/BM25 or structured) using the concrete activity (e.g., 'pet-friendly', 'spot', 'search') before concluding the information is unavailable.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure is a lexical mismatch: the question asked about a 'shared frustration', but the supporting memory stated the concrete situation ('Andrew is searching for a pet-friendly spot and has not found one'), so the literal-word search missed it. The rule to expand emotion-word queries into unmet-need and ongoing-search evidence is reusable for any future question about frustrations, problems, or difficulties, where memories typically record behavior rather than the label.

payload.name: Emotion-location answers need activity-place searches
payload.description: When a question asks which places give a person peace, calm, joy, or similar positive emotion, search using both emotion terms and the person's recurring activities at candidate locations before answering.
content: If the question asks for places/locations that give a person a positive emotion (peace, calm, joy, comfort), run at least two searches: one with the emotion-focused phrasing and one that combines the person's known activities (e.g., yoga, meditation, walking) with candidate place types (beach, park, trail, home, retreat, garden).
Before listing a place in the answer, require a retrieved memory that connects that place to the person AND contains an emotion/calm descriptor, preferring the most recent version of the memory.
When the first search returns only generic places, broaden with location nouns and activity nouns in the query instead of simply increasing top-k or using the same query again.

candidates.solves: Answers to 'which places give a person peace/calm/joy' can be missed when retrieval uses only emotion-focused queries, because these memories may be encoded as an activity performed at a place (e.g., practicing yoga at the beach). The skill applies to any question asking for places linked to a person's positive emotion; it is not needed for questions about static attributes or about activities themselves.

payload.name: Count-event-mentions-with-inflections
payload.description: When a question asks how many times someone performed an activity (won, played, mentioned, etc.), expand keyword searches to cover inflections and singular/plural forms before retrieving memories.
content: For counting questions about past actions, first list morphological variants of the action verb (e.g., win/wins/won/winning) and both singular/plural object nouns (game/games).
Issue keyword searches for each variant and combine with semantic/hybrid search to retrieve memories phrased differently; do not assume a single query captures all mentions.

candidates.solves: The agent missed multiple memory entries because it searched only one keyword inflection ("winning games") while the stored memories used different verb forms and singular nouns ("won", "win a game", "game"). The failure mechanism is over-reliance on a single keyword form when counting repeated actions or events. This applies to any count-of-action question where memories may phrase the action with varied inflections or synonyms, so future searches must expand to all morphological variants and combine keyword with semantic retrieval.

payload.name: Psychological-state synonym search
payload.description: When a question asks how someone stays or becomes confident, motivated, positive, or keeps going, expand retrieval with equivalent mental-state synonyms and strategy-oriented phrases before concluding evidence is missing.
content: If the user asks how a person maintains or achieves a psychological state (e.g., confidence, motivation, positivity), run at least one extra search using synonyms of that state (motivated, encouraged, determined, positive, strong) combined with strategy phrases like 'strategies for staying', 'ways to keep', 'support system', 'goals', 'reasons for starting'.

Treat memories that describe the person's motivation, encouragement, or coping strategies as relevant evidence for confidence-related questions, and do not depend on the exact keyword from the question appearing in the memory.

candidates.solves: When a question asks how a person maintains a psychological state like confidence, retrieval can miss memories that express the same state through different words such as motivation or encouragement. This rule expands the search with synonyms and strategy-oriented phrases and accepts such memories as relevant evidence. It does not apply to factual, non-psychological questions.

payload.name: Implicit inspiration source search
payload.description: When a question asks about what inspires or motivates a person, and the initial search lacks an explicit inspiration memory, run additional searches for achievement, validation, and positive feedback memories.
content: During questions about a person's inspiration or motivation, treat 'validation', 'achievement', 'recognition', and 'positive feedback' as potential inspiration sources; run additional hybrid searches for these terms before concluding.
If an answer claim lacks direct supporting memory and the memory pool contains events about the subject's successes or well-received work, retrieve those events as evidence for implicit inspiration.

After each retrieval round, verify whether the evidence covers all plausible answer components; if a component remains unsupported, issue another search with broader semantic expansions instead of answering immediately.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was a single literal 'inspiration' search that missed a memory where Joanna's work was validated, leaving the 'validation' answer component unsupported. The abstract mechanism is that inspiration sources are often implicit in validation, achievement, or feedback memories, so literal keyword searches are insufficient. This skill applies to any future question asking what a person is inspired or motivated by, regardless of topic, and ensures evidence sufficiency before answering. It does not apply to non-motivational factual questions.

payload.name: Find competing interests for delayed activity
payload.description: When asked why a person sometimes delays, skips, or puts off a regular activity, also search for that person's other hobbies, interests, and preferred activities to explain the behavior.
content: Before answering why someone sometimes delays or omits a recurring activity, run an additional semantic or keyword search for that person's other hobbies, interests, and preferred activities (e.g., query '<person> hobbies and interests').

If the retrieved memories only describe the activity itself or direct mentions of delay, treat evidence as insufficient and expand the search to competing interests; a strong competing interest can explain the delay even if it never mentions the delayed activity.

candidates.solves: When a question asks why someone sometimes delays, skips, or puts off a recurring activity, the runtime searches only for direct delay statements and misses competing hobbies that explain the behavior. Apply when seeking reasons for intermittent non-participation by any person; do not apply to external obstacles, scheduling conflicts, or intrinsic activity drawbacks.

payload.name: Enumeration-Question Synonym-Expanded Searches
payload.description: When a question asks how a person did something and expects a list of actions, use expanded synonym searches to find all action memories before answering.
content: When a question asks 'How did <entity> <outcome>?' or 'What actions did <entity> take?', treat it as an enumeration request whose answer may span multiple distinct activities stored in separate memories.

Before answering, if the initial retrieval returns only some action memories, run additional searches using action-oriented synonyms and paraphrases of the target verb/outcome (e.g., for 'promote': marketing, advertising, partner, collaboration, launch, campaign, showcase, content, video) to surface memories that describe the same activity category with different wording.

Check sufficiency after each search: if the question asks for 'how' and new searches keep finding different actions, continue until no new distinct actions appear; do not finalize an answer after a single top-k retrieval when the question is enumerative.

candidates.solves: One search with only the question's verb can miss memories describing the same activity category in different words (e.g., 'promote' versus 'partnered with an artist', 'limited-edition line', 'video presentation'). The diagnosed agent answered after a single hybrid retrieval, leaving valid action memories out. This applies to any future 'how' / 'what actions' enumeration question: run synonym-expanded searches and verify completeness before answering.

payload.name: Expand_rewarding_experience_queries_with_achievement_terms
payload.description: When a question asks what someone recently did that was rewarding/fulfilling and the first search lacks a clear achievement event, run an additional search with concrete achievement vocabulary (presented, conference, received positive feedback, award, recognized) before answering.
content: If the question uses abstract positive descriptors like 'rewarding experience', 'fulfilling', or 'sense of accomplishment' and the initial retrieval does not return an event memory that explicitly describes an achievement or positive outcome, run an additional keyword or structured search using concrete achievement verbs and nouns (e.g., 'presented', 'conference', 'received positive feedback', 'award', 'recognized').
