Do not answer from the first result set if it lacks a high-confidence direct match; perform this additional search first, and if it yields an achievement event, weigh it above loosely matching experiential activities.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask what someone recently did that was 'rewarding' or 'fulfilling' are often grounded in event memories of achievements or positive feedback, which may not contain the abstract reward vocabulary and therefore can be missed by a single semantic search. This rule triggers an extra targeted retrieval using concrete achievement/recognition terms before answering, and applies to any future question with abstract positive-evaluative wording.

payload.name: Subject-centric retry for theme queries
payload.description: When a question asks about a theme/pattern emerging in one person's life (especially 'as mentioned by another'), and initial hybrid results lack relevant episodic memories, retry with queries on the subject's own interactions/encounters, omitting the abstract theme word and the other person's name.
content: When a question asks about a theme, pattern, or trend emerging in a specific person's life, do not rely only on queries containing the abstract theme word or a mentioner's name; those terms may be absent from stored episodic memories.

If the first hybrid search returns only unrelated general memories, run at least one follow-up search focused on the subject's own recent activities, interactions, and encounters (e.g., subject + 'helping', 'encounters', 'recurring'), and do not include the abstract theme word or the other person's name.

Before answering, verify the retrieved evidence actually reflects the asked theme; if the evidence contains only generic plans, relationships, or unrelated events, continue searching the subject's discrete episodes until a recurring behavioral pattern is found or exhausted.

candidates.solves: When a question asks about a theme or pattern emerging in a person's life (often phrased as 'as mentioned by someone else'), retrieval can fail because the supporting memory describes the subject's concrete recurring interactions without containing the abstract theme word or the mentioner's name. Future such questions should trigger supplementary subject-centric searches that drop abstract labels and mentioner names to surface discrete episodic memories.

payload.name: Recurring-frustration behavioral search expansion
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's recurring frustration, repeated issue, or ongoing problem, expand retrieval from the abstract emotion word to concrete behavior/object plus frequency terms, and prefer explicit recurrence statements as evidence.
content: When a question asks about a person's recurring frustration, repeated issue, or ongoing problem, do not limit searches to the abstract emotion word (e.g., 'frustration', 'annoyance'). Issue follow-up searches combining concrete behavior/object terms implied by the question or by already-retrieved memories with frequency terms such as 'every week', 'weekly', 'always', 'keeps', or 'ritual'.

Before answering with a candidate frustration, check whether a retrieved memory explicitly states the recurrence or pattern (e.g., 'has been doing X on a weekly basis'); prefer that explicit statement as evidence over an indirect, one-time, or jocular mention.

candidates.solves: Questions using abstract emotion words (e.g., 'recurring frustration') often fail to match memories that state the same pattern with concrete behavioral verbs and frequency terms (e.g., 'does X weekly, calls it a ritual'). The retrieval searched only the emotion term and missed a direct, newer memory. This skill requires expanding to concrete behavior/object plus frequency terms for such questions, and preferring an explicit recurrence statement over an indirect or jocular mention. Applies to questions about any user's recurring frustration or repeated issue.

payload.name: Expand searches for stressor questions beyond literal wording
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's main stressor, source of stress, or biggest difficulty, expand retrieval with stress-related synonyms and common life domains before answering.
content: Before answering a question about a person's main stressor, source of stress, or biggest difficulty, issue searches that go beyond the literal question wording: include stress-related synonyms (stressful, tough, difficult, hard, pressure, overwhelmed) and common life domains (work, family, school, health, finances, relationships).

If the question explicitly excludes a topic ('besides X', 'other than X', 'apart from X'), do not let that excluded topic dominate the query; run an additional search replacing the excluded topic with likely alternative domains.
Do not answer from an indirect memory that only implies the stressor through an overlap or trade-off; keep searching until a memory explicitly states what is stressful, tough, or difficult.

candidates.solves: Questions about a person's main stressor or biggest difficulty often miss the directly relevant memory because retrieval anchors on literal wording and any explicitly excluded topic. Expanding searches with stress-related synonyms and common life domains, and refusing indirect evidence, surfaces the explicit statement. Applies to any future question about a person's stressors or difficulties.

payload.name: Relax recipient in recommendation searches
payload.description: When a question asks what one person recommended, suggested, or advised another within a time period and the initial search finds no event, the stored memory may omit the recipient's name.
content: When answering 'what did A recommend/suggest/advise to B in period P?', note that the stored event may name only A and the recommended object, not B.
If the first search returns no matching event, run an additional search using A, action terms (recommend, suggested, must-visit, advised), and the time window P, without B in the query or keywords.

Also try a structured search on predicate types like recommendation with subject A and object category inferred from the question; verify the event's world_start is within P before using it as evidence.

candidates.solves: Stored recommendation events may name only the recommender and object, not the recipient; a recipient-anchored query misses such memories and the agent stops after one search. The rule abstracts that question participants may be absent from memory content: before concluding no information, re-search by action terms plus recommender and time window, dropping the absent recipient. Applies to future who-recommended-what-to-whom questions, not when no such memory exists.

payload.name: Broaden recommendation retrieval beyond recipient and date
payload.description: When a question asks what item one person recommended to another on a specific date and initial searches with both names and the date return no direct match, broaden retrieval before answering.
content: If initial hybrid search for an item recommended by person A to person B on a date returns no memory explicitly naming both A and B or the date, run an additional hybrid search using only A plus the item category (e.g., book, movie, product) with time_mode none, and inspect current versions of top results.

During evidence checking, treat statements that A read, watched, finished, or highly recommends an item as supporting a recommendation even if B and the exact date are absent; do not require all question entities to match.

candidates.solves: A direct search constrained by both named entities and a point-in-time date can miss a current merged memory with a strong recommendation that lacks the recipient and exact date. Broadening to the recommender plus item category, and accepting recommendation statements without full participant/time overlap, recovers such evidence. Applies to any 'what did A recommend to B on date' question when direct retrieval is inconclusive.

payload.name: Retrieve preference memories for subjective questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what a person misses, likes, loves, values, or wants and initial hybrid results only restate behavior; add preference-kind memory retrieval and prefer the newest versions before answering.
content: When the question asks about subjective feelings or preferences (misses, likes, loves, values, wants), run at least one structured memory search filtered to memory_kind=preference for that person, in addition to the hybrid search.

If initial results contain only indirect event/state restatements, issue another search with the person's name and terms like 'misses', 'loves', 'finds soothing', 'prefers', using a higher top_k and inspecting the newest version (highest version_no) of each returned memory ID.
Prefer the content of the newest enriched version of a relevant memory over older versions or indirect paraphrases; answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: Questions about what a person misses, likes, values, or wants can retrieve only indirect event/state memories while newer explicit preference memories are missed. Remedy: include a preference-kind structured search and inspect the newest version of each relevant memory before answering, preferring direct preference evidence over paraphrases. Applies to subjective feeling/preference questions; not to objective factual recalls.

payload.name: Expand recommendation queries to recommender's interest memories
payload.description: When a question asks what A recommends/suggests for B and initial search yields no direct evidence, run additional searches using A's hobbies, preferences, or enjoyed items before answering.
content: If the question asks what one person recommends or suggests for another, first search explicitly for recommendation language, but if the top results lack a direct answer, immediately issue follow-up searches centered on the recommender's own interests, hobbies, or preferences (e.g., with terms like enjoy, plays, likes, favorite).

Before finalizing an answer to a recommendation question, verify you have searched for memories where the recommender is the subject and the predicate is a hobby, preference, or enjoyed activity; such memories often contain the actual recommended items.

When a search returns only tangential relational or planning memories, do not settle on partial evidence; expand top_k or vary query expansions to include the recommender's interest vocabulary before answering.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for recommendations one person gives another, evidence may be stored as the recommender's own hobbies/likes rather than explicit recommendation. Diagnosed: hybrid search for 'games recommended by Jolene for Deborah' missed Jolene's hobby memory with game titles. Before concluding no evidence, search the recommender's interests. Applies to any future recommendation query where target's preferences are in the recommender's memories.

payload.name: Corroborate list-answer items with targeted searches
payload.description: When a question asks for the ways, methods, or items a person uses for an activity, and a retrieved memory mentions a candidate item, run targeted follow-up searches using the item plus the person's name to find corroborating preference or event memories before answering.
content: When a question asks for the ways, methods, or items a person uses for an activity, gather candidate items from both event memories and preference memories (e.g., what the person prefers, likes, or uses).

If a candidate item is supported by only one retrieved memory, run a targeted search using the item term combined with the person's name (e.g., '<person> <item>') to find corroborating or contradicting memories.
Include preference-oriented query variants such as 'prefers', 'likes', 'uses', 'enjoys' alongside action-oriented terms like 'methods', 'ways', 'enhances' when retrieving evidence for such questions.

candidates.solves: Broad action-oriented queries missed a preference memory that supported part of the answer, causing an incomplete list. For list-seeking 'ways/how' questions, each candidate item should be corroborated by a targeted search combining the item with the person's name, since broad queries may miss preference memories. This applies to any future question asking for methods, ways, or items a person uses for an activity.

payload.name: Expand recommendation queries to preference memories
payload.description: When a question asks what games, books, movies, or items one person recommends or would suggest for another, also search for that person's own stated preferences, favorites, likes, hobbies, and enjoyments, not only explicit 'recommend' wording.
content: Before answering a question of the form 'What does X recommend/suggest for Y?', issue at least one search combining X's name with preference vocabulary: 'X enjoys/likes/plays/reads/watches', 'X's favorite', 'X is interested in', or 'X's hobby'. Do not limit expansions to 'recommend' or 'suggest'.

If no retrieved memory explicitly links X's recommendation to Y or directly states the recommended items, search again using the preference phrasing before concluding that evidence is insufficient or answering with a partial result.

When a memory records X's own preferred items in the question's category (e.g., games she plays, books he reads), treat it as candidate evidence for what X would recommend to someone else; verify the category matches and then answer from that evidence.

candidates.solves: Question asks what one person recommends for another, but the agent's single search used only 'recommend/suggest' expansions and missed the target memory recording the person's own game preferences/hobbies. The abstract mechanism is that recommendation questions are often answerable from a person's stated likes and activities, not from explicit recommendation records. This rule instructs retrieval to broaden to preference/hobby vocabulary, applies to any topic category (games, books, movies, restaurants), and does not apply when the recommendation is explicitly recorded.

payload.name: Require explicit preference evidence and multi-query retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for a list of things a person likes/enjoys and the first search yields few or generic results, run multiple targeted preference searches before answering.
content: Before answering a 'what does X like' type question, do not rely on a single incidental event or plan; search for explicit preference statements using terms like 'favorite', 'loves', 'enjoys', 'prefers' combined with category words (e.g., 'food', 'recipe', 'dish', 'meal').

If the first retrieval returns off-topic or only weakly related memories, run follow-up searches for each plausible subcategory, and filter by memory_kind 'preference' when available, until you find multiple explicit mentions or exhaust distinct formulations.
Cite only memories that state or clearly imply the person likes the item; an event alone (e.g., 'plans to order X') is insufficient evidence of a general preference unless corroborated.

candidates.solves: A single generic retrieval returned off-topic memories and the agent answered from one weak incidental event, missing explicit preference records that would have supported a fuller answer. The failure mechanism is stopping retrieval too early and treating an event or plan as if it established a like. This rule applies to any future question asking what a person likes or does not like (foods, activities, books, etc.): retrieve explicit preference evidence via multiple targeted searches before answering.

payload.name: Event evidence for preference queries
payload.description: When a question asks for a person's favorite or preferred items, search event memories of making, eating, or praising the item (delicious, loved, enjoyed) in addition to preference memories.
content: For favorite/preference questions, run an additional search over `event` memories using positive-evaluation terms (e.g., 'found delicious', 'loved', 'enjoyed') together with the item or category.
Treat event memories where the person made or consumed something and responded positively as supporting evidence for a preference, even if the memory is not of kind `preference`.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about someone's favorites or preferences, relying only on `preference` memories can miss event memories where the person made or consumed the item and reacted positively. Future favorite/preference questions should expand retrieval to positive-experience events; this does not apply to purely factual queries that ask for actions or states without an implicit liking.

payload.name: Direction-sensitive recommendation recall
payload.description: Use when a question asks what recommendations, advice, suggestions, or pointers one person received from another, e.g., 'what recommendations has X received from Y?'
content: Before searching, fix the direction: the source is the person who gave; the recipient is the person who received. Build query expansions such as '<source> recommended/advised/suggested to <recipient>' and '<recipient> was recommended/advised by <source>'.
Filter retrieved memories by direction: exclude memories where the recipient recommended, supported, or gave advice to the source; they answer the reverse question.

When the top results are all reverse-direction or supportive-only, run extra searches for '<source> advice to <recipient>' and '<source> inspired <recipient>' and include memories where the recipient's plan or action is explicitly attributed to the source's advice or setup.
Answer only from memories whose evidence assigns the source as the giver and the recipient as the receiver; if none are found, do not substitute reverse-direction memories as evidence.

candidates.solves: When answering what recommendations or advice one person received from another, semantic retrieval often surfaces reverse-direction memories (the recipient recommending to the source) because queries use the shared noun 'recommendation' without directional anchoring. Future questions about directed advice, suggestions, or influence between two people require explicit directional search and evidence filtering so answers include only memories where the named source gave to the named recipient.

payload.name: Implicit-suggestion recall via agreement and plan memories
payload.description: When a question asks what suggestions, recommendations, or advice one person gave another, and initial retrieval returns only general support or encouragement, also search from the recipient's perspective and for plan/event memories of commitments before concluding no evidence exists.
content: When a question asks what suggestions/recommendations/advice one person gave another and the first retrieval returns only general support or encouragement, run additional searches from the recipient's perspective: '<recipient> agreed to try', '<recipient> plans to switch to', '<recipient> is trying', combined with the question's topic keywords.

Also issue a structured search for plan or event memories whose subject is the recipient and whose predicate/object indicates a commitment or change (e.g., dietary_change, switching to, trying), because such memories often imply the giver's suggestion.

Before answering, check that the retrieved evidence actually enumerates the requested items; if it does not, do not answer from general support memories—either search again for the specific items or state the unsupported portion explicitly.

candidates.solves: A question about suggestions or recommendations one person gave another can fail when memories record the recipient's agreement or plan (e.g., 'agreed to try', 'plans to switch to') rather than the giver's explicit wording, so a query for 'A suggested' misses the supporting memory. The reusable rule is to supplement initial retrieval with recipient-perspective queries and structured plan/event searches for commitments, then confirm the evidence enumerates the requested items. This applies to any future advice/suggestion question where the answer may be encoded in plan memories.

payload.name: Structured-search speaker statements
payload.description: When a question asks what a specific person said, recommended, or described about a specific place or topic, first run a structured search with subject set to that person and add descriptive query expansions before concluding no information.
content: When the question asks what a specific person said, recommended, or described about a specific place or topic, run a structured search with subject set to that person's name and a query containing the place/topic and its common synonyms or abbreviations.
Include at least one query expansion using likely descriptive language from stored memories (e.g., adjectives like 'amazing', nouns like 'culture', 'food') in addition to rephrasing the question.
If the first search yields no directly relevant result, retry with increased top_k (10-15) or a keyword-only search before answering 'No information available'.

candidates.solves: Solves retrieval failures when a question asks what a specific person said about a place/topic, but the memory is stored as an event with the speaker as subject and uses descriptive vocabulary absent from the question. The rule triggers a structured subject filter and descriptive expansions before 'no information'. Applies to attributed-statement questions; not to generic factual queries.

payload.name: Supplement searches for item lists across related contexts
payload.description: When a question asks for all items a person uses or prefers during an activity, run supplementary searches with related context terms and aggregate distinct items from all retrieved memories before answering.
content: If the question asks for all items (music, books, foods, etc.) tied to an activity, do not answer from one exact-match retrieval. Run at least one additional search using related context terms such as meditation, relaxation, calming, focus, or associated settings.

When returning an item list, include distinct named items found in preference and event memories even if the memory says recommended, suggested, or calming rather than directly used during the activity.
Before finalizing, check whether the combined results cover all plausible named items from the related contexts; if a related-context search is still missing, refine keywords and search again.

candidates.solves: A question asks for all items (e.g., music tracks, books, foods) a person associates with an activity. A single exact-match search can return only memories whose wording directly names that activity, while another relevant memory describes the same item through a related context such as meditation, relaxation, or calm. The skill requires supplementary searches using related activity terms and aggregation of distinct named items across preference/event memories before answering.

payload.name: Preference-verb retrieval for recommendation questions
payload.description: When a question asks what a person suggested/recommended and initial search with recommendation verbs yields no clear evidence, run another search with the person's name plus preference verbs (enjoys, likes, plays, favorite) and context terms.
content: If the question asks about a suggestion/recommendation and the initial retrieval lacks a memory that explicitly names the recommended item, do not answer from a partially matching memory.

Run an additional search combining the person's name with preference/activity verbs (enjoys, likes, plays, favorite, particularly) plus the question's context words (platform, category) before answering.
Accept a memory as evidence only if it explicitly associates the named item with the person, even if that association is phrased as a preference rather than a suggestion.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what a person suggested or recommended and the first search with recommendation verbs returns only a partially matching distractor, the correct evidence may be stored as a preference ('enjoys', 'plays') rather than an explicit suggestion. Expanding retrieval with preference verbs surfaces the right memory and prevents premature answers from partial matches; this applies when the fact is about a person's stated likes or activities, not when a direct suggestion event is already in evidence.

payload.name: Shared-activity retrieval for multi-person gift questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a gift, plan, or recommendation suitable for two or more named people, expand retrieval to their shared activities, hobbies, classes, and interests, not just the abstract topic.
content: When the question asks for a gift, plan, or recommendation suitable for two or more named people, run a retrieval that combines their names with concrete shared-activity terms (cooking, recipes, classes, hobbies, outings) in addition to abstract topic keywords.

Before answering, check that the proposed gift is supported by evidence for each intended recipient; if evidence supports only one person, search for a shared activity or interest instead of defaulting to one person's individual preference.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a gift or recommendation suitable for multiple named people, retrieval that uses only abstract topic keywords ('healthy lifestyle gift') can miss concrete shared-activity memories (cooking classes, shared recipes) that support the best answer. Future inputs asking for multi-person gifts, plans, or recommendations should trigger searches over shared activities/hobbies and a per-recipient evidence sufficiency check before answering.

payload.name: Locate events by temporally adjacent location memories
payload.description: When a question asks where a subject performed an activity or found something, and search returns the activity memory without a location, search for the subject's location memories (trips, retreats, visits) around that event's date before answering.
content: Before answering a 'where' question about an activity or discovery, check whether the retrieved evidence names a location. If not, and the event memory has a date, run additional searches for the subject's trips, retreats, visits, or residences with a time window overlapping that date (e.g., same or nearby month), using terms like the subject plus travel/location words.

Do not infer a location from a different, lexically similar activity memory (e.g., a hike discovery when asked about a diving spot) unless that memory explicitly states the location or the same activity. Combine location evidence only when it is temporally consistent with the event date.
When evidence supports a location only by combining an activity memory with a temporally adjacent location memory, answer from that combined evidence and cite both memory IDs.

candidates.solves: A 'where' question about an activity is answered from an event memory lacking location, while the location lives in a separate memory (trip/retreat/visit) sharing no keywords with the activity. The fix is to retrieve location memories temporally adjacent to the event date and only combine them when temporally consistent; do not borrow a location from a different activity memory. Applies to any subject/event where question; not needed when direct evidence names the location.

payload.name: Location-Question Search and Named Place Recognition
payload.description: When a question asks which state/place a person visited during a period/event, run additional searches using the person's name plus location keywords before concluding no evidence, and recognize named geographical entities.
content: When the question asks for a state or geographical location visited by a person during a specified period/event, run an additional hybrid/BM25 search using the person's name plus location-related keywords (e.g., 'mountain', 'city', 'state', 'park', 'at', 'in') before concluding no information.

If a retrieved memory mentions a named geographical entity (mountain, river, city, park), use known facts about that entity's location to answer the state/region, even if the memory does not repeat the event label.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is retrieval failure: queries centered on an event label (e.g., 'internship visit location') miss memories that record a specific location through an activity (e.g., 'practiced yoga on a named mountain') without repeating the event label. The abstract mechanism is that location answers are often encoded in activity memories via named geographical entities, not as explicit state/event terms. This rule applies to any future state/place question where the answer depends on recognizing a named place in a memory and mapping it to a jurisdiction using world knowledge.

payload.name: Implicit-location event retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks which locations a person has been to or visited, after an initial travel-vocabulary search, also search for event memories that imply presence at a place without using explicit travel words.
content: After the initial travel/visit search, if the question asks where a person has been, issue additional event-memory searches targeting implicit presence: combine the person's name with terms like 'in <place>', 'photo', 'conversation', 'met', 'tour', or 'stay'. Do not require the words 'visited' or 'location' to appear.

When judging evidence for a location, treat event memories that describe an activity at a named place (e.g., taking a photo in X, having a conversation in X) as supporting that the person was in that place, even if they lack explicit travel vocabulary.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: relying only on 'visited/locations' terms in a hybrid search missed memories that imply presence at a place without explicit travel vocabulary, such as 'a conversation with a fan in California' and 'took a photo in the Smoky Mountains'. The abstract failure is treating explicit travel verbs as necessary evidence for presence. The rule transfers to any future person/location question by broadening retrieval to implicit-presence events, and it applies whenever the initial results seem incomplete.

payload.name: Visited-places retrieval with visit synonyms and country inference
payload.description: When a question asks which countries or places a person has visited or traveled to, use retrieval that includes visit/been-to synonyms in queries and keywords, and infer countries from city or region mentions.
content: When a question asks which countries or places a person has visited, run searches using both travel and visit vocabulary ('visited', 'has been to', 'went to') in queries, expansions, and keywords; do not rely only on 'travel' or 'country'.
Do not restrict searches to memories whose text contains 'country'; also search for destination names such as cities or regions, since a city/region visit may be the only memory supporting a country.
Before answering a country-level question, normalize destination granularity: treat a retrieved city or region as evidence of its country, and never answer with the city/region itself as a country.

If a retrieved destination is a non-country place, use it as a lead to search for country-level evidence; if none exists, acknowledge the granularity gap rather than presenting the place as a country.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that country/place questions failed because retrieval used only travel/country keywords, missing event memories phrased with 'visited [city]', and the final answer reported a non-country destination. The abstract mechanism is vocabulary mismatch and destination-granularity mismatch in visited-place retrieval. This applies to any future question asking which countries or places someone has visited, where memories may mention cities or regions instead of country names.

payload.name: Time-filtered_retrieval_before_no_information
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's travel or activity in a specific month/year and the initial search returns no relevant evidence, perform a structured search for events with a world_start within that period before answering no information.
content: If a question specifies a person and a time period (month/year) and the initial search yields no directly relevant memory, issue a structured search for events with a world_start falling within that time period, using the person's name as the subject.

Before concluding 'no information available', ensure that at least one time-filtered search has been attempted, and incorporate travel-related synonyms (trip, road trip, visited, went to) if the question asks about travel or locations.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about a person's travel or activity in a specific month/year and the initial retrieval returns no relevant memory, the agent often stops and answers 'no information' even though a relevant event exists but uses different wording (e.g., 'road trip' vs. 'travel'). This skill applies to any temporal question about a person's activities, instructing the agent to run an additional structured search filtered to the specified time period before concluding no evidence exists.

payload.name: Expand country visit queries to major cities and infer visits
payload.description: When retrieving memories to answer how many times someone has visited a country, query for that country and its major cities, and interpret any memory of being in a city as evidence of visiting the country.
content: Before answering a question about visits to a specific country, run additional searches using the country name plus related city names, landmarks, or regions known to be in that country.

When reviewing retrieved memories, treat any memory stating the person was in a city or location within the country as evidence of a visit to that country, even if the country name is not explicitly mentioned.
Count each distinct time the person was present at such a city or location as a separate visit, using memory timestamps or events to separate occurrences.

candidates.solves: When answering questions about how many times a person has visited a country, the runtime often limits retrieval to memories containing the country name and misses memories that mention cities within that country, even though being in a city implies being in the country. This also causes the model to fail to interpret retrieved city-based memories as evidence of country visits. This rule applies to any future question asking for visit counts or travel history to a country where memories may reference cities or regions instead of the country name.

payload.name: Geographic-inference retrieval for region questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a state, province, or country associated with a person's visit or activity, and the exact region name does not appear in retrieved memories, expand search to include cities/landmarks and treat a city/landmark memory as evidence for its containing region.
content: If the question asks for a state, province, or country and the first search returns no memory naming that exact region, rerun the search using likely city or landmark names inside that region and also as generic keyword expansions without the region name.

When judging whether retrieved evidence answers a region question, treat a memory that mentions a city or well-known location as evidence for the state/province/country that contains it; do not answer 'no information' solely because the exact region label is absent.

candidates.solves: A retrieval or answer step fails when a question asks for a broad geographical unit (state, province, country) and the supporting memory mentions only a city or landmark inside that unit, so the exact region name is absent from the query and results. The fix is to make retrieval and evidence evaluation geography-aware: rerun with sub-region names and infer the containing region from a retrieved city/landmark. It does not apply when the requested region name already appears in a retrieved memory.

payload.name: List-mention retrieval across event memories
payload.description: When a question asks which places/entities a person mentioned, use event and plan memories as candidate sources and run expanded queries with entity names, not just the question's verbs.
content: If the question asks to list places/entities that a person mentioned, do not search only the question's verb (e.g., 'visit', 'travel'). Also run queries combining the person's name with event/plan terms (e.g., 'game in', 'trip to') and with the entity type (e.g., 'cities').
When structured search is available, filter by subject=person and memory_kind in (event, plan), then scan content for the entity names; treat future events as valid mentions.

Before answering, perform a second pass: for each entity already found, run a query for that entity name with the person's name to catch additional memories that might use it without the question verb.

candidates.solves: The runtime missed a relevant memory about an upcoming event in Seattle because the search used only 'visit/travel' expansions, while the memory described an event (basketball game) rather than an explicit visit. The abstraction is that list-questions about mentioned entities require searching across memory kinds and verb variants, including events and plans, and verifying with entity-based fallback queries. This applies to any 'which X does person mention' question where the mentions may be implicit in event/plan memories.

payload.name: CompleteAffectedGroupMemberSearches
payload.description: When a question asks who in a family or group was injured, hurt, sick, or otherwise affected, expand searches across member roles and condition synonyms before answering.
content: When a question asks which members of a family or group were affected (injured, hurt, sick, in an accident, etc.), treat it as a completeness query: after any hit, run additional searches pairing each known or role-based member (son, daughter, partner, spouse, child, friend) with condition synonyms (accident, injury, ankle, hospital, doctor, illness, therapy).

Before giving a final answer, verify that you have searched for all plausible group members and alternate phrasings; if the evidence covers only one member or one wording, continue searching rather than answering.

candidates.solves: When a question asks which members of a family or group were injured or otherwise affected, a single lexical search often misses a relevant memory because the event is phrased differently (e.g., 'soccer accident' vs. 'injured'). This rule requires member-aware query expansion and a completeness check before answering; it applies to any group-condition retrieval question and is not needed for single-subject queries.

payload.name: Synonym-expand damage queries before no-info
payload.description: Apply when a question asks what items or possessions a person had broken, damaged, or had issues with; expand searches with synonyms and event-type terms before answering.
content: When a question asks about things a person had broken, damaged, or had issues with, expand the search with concept synonyms such as 'broke down', 'accident', 'crash', 'damage', 'malfunction', 'issue', 'problem', or 'not working', not only the literal word from the question.

If the initial results contain no damage-related memories, run a follow-up search using the person's name plus likely object categories (e.g., vehicle, car, possession) and, when available, filter by structured event predicates like accident, breakdown, or vehicle issues.
Do not answer 'No information available' after a single unhelpful result set; re-search with varied synonyms first and only conclude no evidence after multiple attempts.

candidates.solves: The access agent ran a single keyword search for 'broken', missed memories describing 'accident' and 'broke down', and prematurely answered 'No information available'. The reusable mechanism is insufficient concept-level query expansion before a negative conclusion; the rule applies to questions about broken, damaged, or faulty possessions, not to metaphorical 'broken' (e.g., promises, hearts).

payload.name: Per-subject enumeration for experience questions
payload.description: When a question asks what experiences or incidents (health scares, trips, problems) named people had, enumerate events per named subject with structured and expanded searches before answering.
content: When a question asks what events or incidents one or more named people experienced (e.g., health scares, trips, problems), run a separate targeted search for each named person instead of relying only on a combined multi-person query; merge unique findings across subjects.

When the question uses a broad category label that may not match memory wording, also run a structured search per named subject constrained to the relevant memory kind (e.g., event) and supplement with concrete sub-terms, because relevant events can be stored under specific vocabulary and rank below the top-k of a hybrid query.

candidates.solves: Category-word questions can miss stored events recorded under concrete vocabulary: a 'health scares' query retrieved two of three health events because one used 'heart palpitation' and a combined two-person query ranked it below top-k. This transfers to any multi-subject, category-level experience question: per-subject and structured enumeration prevents incomplete answers.

payload.name: Require Named Answers for Specific-Entity Questions
payload.description: When a question asks which/what specific ailment, disease, dish, place, or other named entity (rather than a category), apply before answering: generic category evidence is insufficient; search for a memory that explicitly names the entity.
content: When the question requests a specific named entity (e.g., 'which ailment', 'what disease', 'which restaurant'), treat generic category terms (e.g., 'health risk', 'discomfort') as insufficient evidence.

If current evidence lacks the named entity, run additional searches combining the subject's name with terms like 'experienced', 'diagnosed', 'visited', or use a structured search for event memories with a related predicate, before issuing an answer.
Answer with a named entity only if it appears verbatim in retrieved memory content; otherwise continue searching rather than settling for a general description.

candidates.solves: An agent answering 'which ailment does X face' answered with a generic 'health risk' because retrieved memories described X's health category but never named the actual condition. The abstract rule is to require verbatim named evidence whenever the question demands a specific entity, and continue searching for event memories containing that name before answering. This applies to future 'which/what' questions about concrete entities (ailments, diseases, places, dishes); it does not apply to questions seeking category-level descriptions or when no memory names the entity.

payload.name: ConcreteTermQueryExpansion
payload.description: When a question contains an abstract or superordinate term, expand the search with concrete specific terms for that category and re-search if initial results are irrelevant.
content: Identify abstract or superordinate words in the question (e.g., 'physical transformation', 'achievement', 'illness') and add concrete hyponyms or descriptors likely to appear in memory (e.g., hair, weight, tournament, injury).
If the first search returns topics unrelated to the abstract category, run additional searches using those concrete expansions before concluding no information.
Use synonyms and category members to cover different wordings of the same fact.

candidates.solves: Retrieval fails when a question uses an abstract category (e.g., 'physical transformation') but memory stores the fact with concrete words (e.g., 'dyed his hair'). This rule prompts concrete-hyponym expansion and a re-search before concluding no information. It applies to any abstract-category retrieval (appearance, achievements, health, etc.) and does not apply when the query already contains the exact concrete terms.

payload.name: Expand submission-target synonyms before answering
payload.description: When a question asks for multiple places or targets someone submitted/sent something to, expand the category into concrete synonyms and search each one before answering.
content: If the question asks for destinations or targets of an action (such as places/venues someone submitted or sent work to), generate concrete hyponyms and synonyms of that category (e.g., contest, competition, festival, publication, company) and run one search with each term instead of only the generic category word.
When the question is plural, continue searching until the retrieved evidence covers every distinct instance; do not answer after the first search that yields only one instance.
Answer with the union of distinct instances that have direct evidence, and never state an instance without retrieval support.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a list of destinations/targets for an action, a query with only the generic category term can miss memories naming specific instances (e.g., 'contest' vs 'places'). This skill triggers synonym/hyponym expansion and repeated searches until every instance implied by the plural question is supported. Not applicable when one retrieval already fully answers a single-fact question.

payload.name: Expand search for course/workshop/group memberships
payload.description: When a question asks what classes, courses, workshops, seminars, groups, or clubs a person joined or attended, search with each activity-type noun variant in separate targeted queries.
content: If the question asks which classes, courses, workshops, seminars, groups, or clubs a person has joined or attended, do not stop after one broad hybrid search.

Issue additional targeted searches that pair the person and topic with each concrete activity-type noun: 'workshop', 'course', 'class', 'seminar', 'group', 'club'; keep searching until all noun variants are exhausted or evidence is sufficient.

candidates.solves: A single broad hybrid search missed stored event memories whose names use concrete nouns like 'workshop' or 'course' when the question only used generic terms like 'classes or groups'. Future questions asking about any courses, workshops, classes, seminars, or groups a person joined can trigger targeted noun-variant searches, avoiding this recall failure across any topic.

payload.name: Retrieve multi-topic merged memories for enumerative coping questions
payload.description: When a question asks what helped a person cope, grieve, or find peace, decompose it into per-facet searches and include keyword/BM25 to catch long multi-topic merged memories that one semantic top-k may miss.
content: When a question asks what helped someone cope, grieve, or find peace, do not rely on a single broad semantic top-k search; decompose the question into distinct facets (practices, places, objects) and run a separate search for each facet.

Long merged memories that combine several topics dilute semantic relevance and can fall below the cutoff; when a facet lacks evidence, run a keyword or BM25 search with that facet's distinctive terms and inspect merged multi-topic versions.
Before finalizing an enumerative answer, ensure every plausible facet has supporting evidence or an explicit search attempt; treat the first semantic result set as non-exhaustive.

candidates.solves: A single semantic search missed a multi-topic merged memory linking yoga to grief-comfort because merged memories dilute per-topic relevance. For enumerative questions asking what helped a person cope, grieve, or find peace, decompose into per-facet searches and add keyword/BM25 to surface merged memories; not needed when the question targets one narrow, already-evidenced facet.

payload.name: Infer enjoyment from genre preferences
payload.description: Use when a question asks whether someone would enjoy a named author or creative work, and memory may contain that person's genre or style preferences.
content: When a question asks whether a person would enjoy a specific author, book, movie, or other creative work, first retrieve and review the person's genre and style preferences from memory.

If the person's preferred genres are visible in memory, identify the genre of the named author/work and match it against those preferences; explicit memories about that exact author or work are not required for a judgment.

Do not answer 'No information available' when preference evidence exists and the author/work's genre can be reasonably identified; reserve that answer for cases where no preference evidence was found.

candidates.solves: The agent declared 'no information' for a would-enjoy-a-specific-author question despite retrieved genre preferences, because no memory named the author. The rule is to test the candidate work's genre against those preferences and only declare insufficiency when no preference evidence exists. Applies to enjoyment questions for books, films, and music; not factual author queries.

payload.name: Include preference memories when enumerating consumed or favorite items
payload.description: When a question asks what a person has read, watched, liked, or consumed, do not restrict the search to event memories; include preference memories too.
content: If the question asks for a list or factual enumeration of a person's read/watched/liked/consumed items (e.g., books, movies, shows, foods, hobbies), run the initial search without a restrictive memory_kind filter, or explicitly include both 'event' and 'preference' memory kinds.

When the first search only returns vague descriptions or fails to name concrete items, repeat the search with preference memories included and inspect any preference memories returned, since they often hold specific titles and ongoing favorites.

candidates.solves: Access queries that ask what a person has read, watched, liked, or otherwise consumed often fail when the initial search is restricted to event memories only, because preference memories frequently store the concrete item names, ongoing reading/listening details, and favorites. The reusable rule is to include preference (and other relevant) memory kinds in the search before answering such enumeration questions. This applies to any future question about books, movies, media, foods, hobbies, or similar preference-laden facts about a person.

payload.name: Include event memories for current-activity queries
payload.description: When a query asks what someone is currently reading, doing, working on, or otherwise engaged in, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'state'; search both 'state' and 'event' memories because ongoing activities are often stored as events.
content: If a question asks about a person's current activity (e.g., currently reading, working on, building, studying), set memory_kinds to include both 'state' and 'event', or omit the memory_kinds filter, since ongoing activities are typically stored as event memories.
If a search restricted to 'state' returns no supporting evidence for an activity question, retry with broader memory_kinds before answering 'no information available'.

candidates.solves: Access failed because the search restricted memory_kinds to 'state', while the requested fact (a current reading activity) was stored as an 'event' memory, so the supporting memory was filtered out and never returned. The reusable rule is to include event memories when a query asks about an ongoing activity, and to broaden the memory-kind filter if a restricted search yields no supporting evidence. This applies to future questions about what a person is currently reading, working on, building, studying, or otherwise engaged in.

payload.name: Retrieve preference memories for ideal/preference questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone thinks an ideal or preferred version of something should be, search for preference-kind memories and use attribute-level query terms before answering.
content: When the question asks for a person's ideal, preferred, or envisioned version of an entity (e.g., ideal studio, dream home, perfect setup), run a structured memory search with memory_kind='preference' in addition to the general hybrid search.

Use attribute-level query terms in expansions that target concrete features of the entity (e.g., flooring, location, lighting, layout, materials) because preference memories often describe specific attributes rather than the general topic.

If the initial top-k results contain only event/state memories about the entity and the question targets desired attributes, run at least one additional search with a higher top-k or a preference-focused query before answering.

candidates.solves: The search missed a preference memory that contained the concrete attribute (e.g., flooring) while retrieving only event/state memories about the person's ongoing project, causing an incomplete answer. Future preference/ideal questions require an explicit preference-kind search with attribute-level terms; do not apply to factual or activity questions without preference words.

payload.name: Search projects across plan and event memory kinds
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, or future intentions, do not restrict search to plan memories alone; include event and other memory kinds that may describe projects or interests.
content: When the question asks about someone's projects, plans, or what they want to do, search across both 'plan' and 'event' memory kinds; projects and intentions are often stored as events with predicate 'project'.

If a first search with memory_kinds=['plan'] returns only tangential results, rerun with a broader kind set (e.g., plan, event, state) and include keywords from the question's subject and domain before answering.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed a retrieval failure where restricting memory_kinds to 'plan' missed event memories describing the same subject's projects. The rule generalizes to any question about a person's projects, plans, or future intentions: such information can be stored under different memory kinds, so the agent must not over-constrain by kind and should re-search more broadly before answering.

payload.name: Include preference memories for favorite/attribute queries
payload.description: When a question asks about someone's favorite, preference, or personal attribute, do not restrict search to event memories; include preference memories before answering.
content: When retrieving evidence for questions about someone's favorite, preferred, or personal attribute (e.g., favorite recipe, food, hobby), include the 'preference' memory kind in the search; do not limit memory_kinds to 'event'.

If the first result set lacks explicit preference statements, issue a follow-up search using memory_kinds containing 'preference' and, when available, structured filters on the subject or predicate before concluding evidence is insufficient.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was restricting retrieval to event memories, so an explicit preference memory was missed and the agent answered from a less specific event. This rule applies to any future question asking about a person's favorite, preferred, or other personal attribute, where the answer may live in a preference memory rather than an event. It does not apply when the question explicitly asks about an event or action.

payload.name: Entity-name questions: retry with attribute-free query
payload.description: When a question asks to identify an entity by descriptive attributes and a date, and the direct search with those attributes fails to return a memory naming the entity, retry a minimal query before answering.
content: When the question asks to name an entity (e.g., a game, movie, book) from descriptive attributes and a date, and the initial hybrid or keyword search does not return any memory containing a plausible entity of that type, retry with a minimal query containing only the subject, the entity type, and the date/date range (e.g., 'game' + date), omitting the descriptive adjectives that may not appear verbatim in stored memories.

If the fallback returns a memory that mentions several activities or titles for that period, inspect it and select the entity whose type matches the question, even if the memory describes the activity as 'mentioned', 'enjoyed', or 'watched' rather than with the question's exact wording.

candidates.solves: When a user asks to name an entity (game, movie, book, etc.) from descriptive attributes and a date, the memory holding the answer often stores the entity name without those literal attribute words, so keyword and semantic searches using the attributes miss it. This skill triggers when an initial attribute-based search yields no entity-naming candidate; it applies to any future entity-identification question regardless of topic, and should not be used when the attributes already appear verbatim in retrieved memories.

payload.name: Search plan and event kinds for future-plan questions
payload.description: When answering questions about future events, planned activities, or what someone is planning for an upcoming time, include plan memories in retrieval; do not restrict memory_kinds to event only.
content: If the question asks about a future event, plan, or upcoming activity, search with memory_kinds covering both 'plan' and 'event' (for example ["plan", "event"]).
Do not filter memory_kinds to only 'event' for forward-looking questions; planned future events are often stored as 'plan' memories.
Before answering, check whether an additional retrieval over 'plan' memories could supply direct evidence, especially when initial results contain only related context.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about a future event or activity, such as what someone is planning for an upcoming season, retrieval that restricts memory_kinds to only 'event' can miss the relevant memory because forward-looking information may be stored as a 'plan'. This rule applies to future-plan questions: include both 'plan' and 'event' memory kinds during retrieval instead of narrowing to event-only searches.

payload.name: Relational-role to meeting-event retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks when a subject first met a person identified only by a relational role (future wife, fiancée, partner, spouse) and direct role-based hits are missing, apply this retrieval pattern.
content: Before answering 'no information,' when the question uses a relational role label for a person, expand searches to include meeting/encounter verbs (met, met up, went on a trip/date with) and descriptive terms from other memories that could identify that person (nationality, names, attributes).

If a later relationship memory is found (marriage, engagement, pregnancy, partner status), use it to identify the person, then search for the earliest meeting or trip event before that memory's date and report that event's time as the meeting.
Only a memory that explicitly describes the meeting or first encounter can establish the meeting time; do not infer it from the later relationship event alone.

candidates.solves: When a question identifies a person only by a relational role (future wife, spouse) and direct role-based retrieval fails, stored memories may describe the meeting by other attributes (nationality, trip partner). Expand retrieval to meeting/encounter terms and person descriptors, then chain from later relationship events to the earliest meeting. Do not infer meeting time from later relationship events alone.

payload.name: Include plan memory kind for future-planning questions
payload.description: When a question asks when or whether someone is planning, intending, or scheduling something in the future, search with memory_kinds including 'plan' and 'event' rather than 'event' only.
content: When the question asks about future plans (e.g., 'when is X planning...', 'does X plan/intend to...', 'what is X planning...'), do not restrict memory_kinds to ['event']; include 'plan' so planned future dates are retrieved.
If a retrieved 'plan' memory specifies the time of the planned activity, prefer it as evidence over a loosely matching 'event' (e.g., a get-together) when the question describes the planned event.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: search restricted memory_kinds to 'event' and missed the 'plan' memory holding the planned reunion date. Future pattern: questions about planned/future activities ('planning', 'plans', 'scheduled', 'intends') should include 'plan' in memory_kinds and prefer a matching plan over a similar event. Does not apply to questions about past/completed events, where 'event' kind suffices.

payload.name: PersonalAttributeLifeStageInference
payload.description: When asked about a person's age or other personal attribute and direct memory lacks the answer, use life-stage cues in retrieved or additional searches (education, work, relationship) to give a bounded uncertain inference instead of replying 'no information'.
content: When a user asks for a personal attribute (age, occupation, marital status) and no memory directly states it, run additional searches using related life-stage terms (e.g., for age: school, study, classes, finals, internship, graduate; for occupation: work, job, career; for marital status: partner, married, spouse).

Treat life-stage cues found in retrieved memories (e.g., attending classes, studying for finals, interning) as evidence for a bounded inference about the attribute, and express the uncertainty explicitly (e.g., 'likely in her 20s or early 30s, since she is in school').
Only answer 'no information available' after both direct and indirect life-stage searches fail to surface any relevant evidence.

candidates.solves: Direct attribute questions (e.g., age) fail because the agent stops after a literal keyword search and ignores implicit life-stage evidence in retrieved memories (student, intern, studying). The abstract mechanism is failing to map an attribute question to indirect evidence cues and to make a clearly-uncertain bounded inference. This applies to any future question about a personal attribute where memory contains contextual life-stage facts.

payload.name: Search both plan and event kinds for scheduled activities
payload.description: When a question asks what someone planned or will do on a specific date, search both plan and event memory kinds; do not restrict memory_kinds to plan only.
content: When searching for what someone planned or scheduled to do on a specific date, set memory_kinds to include both 'plan' and 'event' because plans may be stored as events, especially after rescheduling or when involving other people.
If a first search with a narrow memory_kinds filter returns only low-relevance results, broaden the filter to include 'event' before concluding the memory is absent.
When memory_kinds is not essential to disambiguate, prefer omitting the filter or including all plausible kinds instead of defaulting to a single kind.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask what people planned to do on a specific date can fail when retrieval restricts memory_kinds to 'plan' while the relevant memory is stored under 'event' (e.g., after rescheduling). This rule applies whenever the memory schema allows the same real-world plan to be recorded under multiple kinds; it is unnecessary if the store guarantees one canonical kind for all plans.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for ownership-duration questions
payload.description: When a question asks how long a person has had, owned, or possessed something, include profile and relationship memory kinds; do not restrict search to event memories only.
content: If the question asks how long someone has had/owned/possessed something (duration, since when, for how many years), run at least one search that includes memory_kinds profile and relationship in addition to event; ownership durations are often stored as profile facts.
If the first search returns only activity/event memories, broaden memory_kinds to include profile and relationship before concluding the fact is absent.

This skill guides the access agent to broaden memory kinds so duration/possession facts are retrieved. It applies to any future possession-duration or attribute-age question, not to event-recall questions about when a specific acquisition happened.

payload.name: Include event memories when searching for projects or plans
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, or goals for an upcoming period, retrieve memories with kind 'event' or 'plan' and do not filter solely on memory_kind 'plan'.
content: Before searching for a person's plans or projects, do not restrict memory_kinds to only 'plan'. Include 'event' memories because projects and aspirations are often stored as events with predicate 'project'.

If the question targets future or upcoming activities, do not exclude memories based on narrow time windows; verify against world_start within the relevant period and consider memories without explicit end dates.

candidates.solves: When a user asks what projects or plans a person has for a future period, retrieval may fail because the search restricts memory_kind to 'plan' while the target memories are stored as 'event' with predicate 'project'. The rule is to include both 'event' and 'plan' kinds and optionally filter on predicate 'project' when searching for projects or goals.
